title: When the launch date is put before the user
summary: A real-life fable of deadlines and technology getting ahead of the people they were meant to serve.
role: Product design, experience research, scoping and user requirements
collaboration: Service design and an applied AI specialist
outcome: The work produced requirements for both experiences, a traced accuracy failure, customer feedback drafts, measured response-time improvements, and working streaming. I also secured customer usage tracking. Customer engagement fell after early interest. Internal adoption stayed low. Representatives reported wrong answers, waiting, and a poor fit with their workflow. Tracking and feedback described the experience; they did not isolate the effect of each feature.

papers.title: Generative AI at Work
papers.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey R. Raymond
papers.finding: Across 5,179 support agents, newer and lower-skilled workers saw larger productivity gains. Suggested replies and relevant documents appeared beside the conversation.
papers.application: Design implication: keep the reference and editable draft beside the task, with the representative in control.
papers.limit: The findings concern one software-support setting. They do not predict results for this project.

papers.title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.finding: In an experiment with 444 participants doing professional writing tasks, ChatGPT shortened task times and raised output ratings.
papers.application: Design implication: make editing and checking the draft part of the workflow before anyone sends it.
papers.limit: These were bounded writing tasks. They do not establish safe answers to account questions.

papers.title: Source quality and editable answers
papers.authors: Luke Wroblewski; Sarah Gibbons, Tarun Mugunthan, and Jakob Nielsen (NN/g)
papers.finding: Luke Wroblewski found that large, poorly parsed PDFs could crowd out useful sources. NN/g observed people repeatedly expanding and shortening answers, then struggling to recover and edit useful passages.
papers.application: Design implication: check extracted content, keep sources visible, and let people edit selected passages without regenerating the whole reply.
papers.limit: Design exploration and an eight-person usability study; neither establishes results for this project.

waiting.heading: User requirements: response time and failure
paragraphs: A service conversation cannot stop while the software thinks. During usability testing and QA, responses averaged about 15 seconds and sometimes took up to 60 seconds.

We measured from the user’s action to the API, then followed the API request and the steps behind it. Working back from the interaction showed where the wait accumulated. Backend changes brought average responses down to roughly 8–10 seconds, at the upper edge of what I considered acceptable for this task.

Streaming was also a requirement for system feedback. Turning it on took a technical lift on the platform we had adopted. We pushed hard for it and got it working, so people could see an answer arrive instead of waiting for the whole reply.
waiting.measurementNote: Measured during project usability testing and QA, as reported by Jacob. Original logs, sample size, and the test window are not retained in this portfolio.
waiting.requirements: Alongside that technical work, I specified acknowledgment within 0.1–0.4 seconds, a holding message at three seconds, and an update at seven. At ten seconds, or immediately after a stall or critical error, offer a route to help.
waiting.note: The replay shows those feedback requirements. Its timer is separate from the measured response times above.

originalDrafts.heading: Feedback that lets the conversation continue
originalDrafts.intro: The original feedback drafts proposed a way to rate an answer, explain a problem and keep asking. People needed useful answers. The business needed to understand where an answer had failed.

steps.heading: Rate the answer
steps.body: Give a thumbs-up or thumbs-down, with the option to change the rating.

steps.heading: Explain, if useful
steps.body: After a thumbs-down, offer an optional explanation.

steps.heading: Keep asking
steps.body: Let the person skip feedback and continue the conversation.

originalDrafts.review: My review framework followed the trigger, feedback, guidance, and completion of each interaction, in the person’s context and on their device. Acceptance criteria included error recovery and tracking.

cards.heading: Learn while serving
cards.body: New staff needed to learn; experienced staff needed to move faster. Both needed accurate, compliant answers within the service conversation.

blocks.text: Usability starts with the system. If the car does not start, we do not go anywhere.
I led experience research and scoping for one conversational assistant in two settings: a public website and the workspace used by service and account-management representatives.

XD/UX belonged in discovery, where we could shape the problem and the requirements. I absorbed the emerging research, worked through the source material with an applied AI specialist, and brought familiar interaction patterns into a new kind of interface.
Accuracy: Give people an answer they can trust. Know when the available material cannot support one.
Compliance: Respect the limits of the service. Route account-specific questions to the person who can answer them.
Speed: Keep pace with the conversation. Help new staff learn and experienced staff get through the work.
Discovery started with the source material
User requirements came before technical requirements. A useful answer depended on the whole system: what it could read, how it used that material, and what happened when it could not help.
Training material lived in PDFs, images, slide decks, Word documents, old scans, and people’s heads. Getting it into a warehouse did not make it fit for answering a customer.
A balance question exposed the problem. The assistant returned 150,000 from a sample account statement. It had treated an example as the customer’s account information.

No balance should have been returned. The only acceptable response was to refer the customer to their account representative. I traced the answer to its source and made that boundary a user requirement.
Learning while the field was moving
The research gave us questions to test. Could assistance shorten the work? Could it carry knowledge to a new hire? What would an experienced representative need to trust or reject a suggestion?

I applied that reading to both experiences: visible system feedback and a route to help for customers; context, references, and review for representatives. Familiar controls still had a job to do. A text box alone could not carry the whole service.
The references below cover research and design explorations published during 2023 and 2024; later work belongs to the continuing investigation.
User requirements: response time and failure
A service conversation cannot stop while the software thinks. During usability testing and QA, responses averaged about 15 seconds and sometimes took up to 60 seconds.

We measured from the user’s action to the API, then followed the API request and the steps behind it. Working back from the interaction showed where the wait accumulated. Backend changes brought average responses down to roughly 8–10 seconds, at the upper edge of what I considered acceptable for this task.

Streaming was also a requirement for system feedback. Turning it on took a technical lift on the platform we had adopted. We pushed hard for it and got it working, so people could see an answer arrive instead of waiting for the whole reply.
Measured during project usability testing and QA, as reported by Jacob. Original logs, sample size, and the test window are not retained in this portfolio.

Alongside that technical work, I specified acknowledgment within 0.1–0.4 seconds, a holding message at three seconds, and an update at seven. At ten seconds, or immediately after a stall or critical error, offer a route to help.
The replay shows those feedback requirements. Its timer is separate from the measured response times above.
Feedback that lets the conversation continue
The original customer flow connected two needs. People needed useful answers and a way to flag a problem. The business needed to understand where the answer had failed.

My review framework followed the trigger, feedback, guidance, and completion of each interaction, in the person’s context and on their device. Acceptance criteria included error recovery and tracking.
Editorial paraphrase of the original customer feedback drafts. The cards show the proposed flow.
An assistant inside the representative’s work
The internal assistant had two jobs: help new staff learn and help experienced staff work faster. Both groups needed accurate, compliant answers without leaving the service conversation.

I scoped the experience around the service workspace: basic account context, a summary of the conversation, sources beside the draft, and follow-up prompts. The representative would read, change, and send the reply.

Document lookup and sharing, an adjacent PDF viewer, suggested wording, compliance warnings, and suspicious-pattern detection formed the future feature set. These added help around the conversation while leaving judgment with the person handling it.
What the work proved, and what happened next

The work produced requirements for both experiences, a traced accuracy failure, customer feedback drafts, measured response-time improvements, and working streaming. I also secured customer usage tracking.
The launch did not include the broader guidance, referral, context, and review experience described here. The future document and alerting concepts remained proposals.

Customer engagement fell after early interest. Internal adoption stayed low. Representatives reported wrong answers, waiting, and a poor fit with their workflow. Tracking and feedback described the experience; they did not isolate the effect of each feature.

The technical work mattered. So did the work around it: the source material, the point at which a person could judge an answer, and the route out when the system could not help. Bringing XD/UX into discovery made those system requirements visible while there was still time to act on them.
New technology gives design more to investigate. The job is still to make it useful to the person using it.

heroSummary: I brought user requirements into discovery for a conversational assistant. Accuracy, speed and the fit with people’s work became the test of what we were building.
